notes.b: Photosynthesis is how plants make their own food. They capture energy from light and use it to build glucose, a sugar, out of two simple substances they take from their surroundings: carbon dioxide and water.
points: Green plants, algae and some bacteria, such as cyanobacteria, photosynthesise. They use light energy, absorbed by the green pigment chlorophyll, to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, and they release oxygen as a by-product.

Because they make their own food from simple inorganic substances, these organisms are called autotrophs (self-feeders). Animals and fungi can't do this, so they must eat food that was made by an autotroph.

The key change is an energy conversion: light energy becomes chemical energy, stored in the bonds of the glucose molecule. Almost every food chain starts with this conversion, so nearly all the energy living things use was first captured by photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis is also where the oxygen in the air comes from. Without it, there would be no oxygen for aerobic respiration.
Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light energy and chlorophyll written above the arrow, because both are needed for the reaction but neither is a reacting substance.

Balanced equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, with light energy and chlorophyll above the arrow. Each side has 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 18 oxygen atoms. Six CO₂ molecules are needed because each one supplies one of glucose's six carbon atoms.
notes.tip: Learn the balanced equation exactly, with light energy and chlorophyll above the arrow. If asked to name the type of nutrition, the answer is autotrophic.

notes.h: Why photosynthesis is an anabolic process
notes.b: Every reaction in a cell either builds molecules up or breaks them down. Photosynthesis is a building-up reaction, and the exam expects you to say why in two parts.
points: An anabolic reaction builds a large molecule from smaller ones and takes in energy to do it. Photosynthesis fits both parts of that definition.
First, it builds a large organic molecule, glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆), from small inorganic molecules, carbon dioxide and water.
Second, it takes in energy rather than releasing it. The energy comes from light, and it ends up stored in the glucose.
Respiration is the opposite, catabolic process: it breaks glucose back down into carbon dioxide and water and releases the stored energy. There is more on this in Respiration as a catabolic process.
notes.tip: For full marks on "why is photosynthesis anabolic?" give both halves: small molecules are built into a larger one, and energy (from light) is taken in.

notes.h: Where the reactants come from and where the products go
notes.b: A plant has to gather carbon dioxide, water and light, and then deal with the oxygen and glucose it makes. Each one has a definite route into or out of the leaf.
points: Carbon dioxide diffuses from the air into the leaf through the stomata, small pores found mainly on the lower surface. It moves through the air spaces inside the leaf to the mesophyll cells, where photosynthesis happens. Some also comes from the plant's own respiring cells.
Plants that live under water can't take gas from the air, so they absorb carbon dioxide dissolved in the water, partly as hydrogencarbonate ions.

Water is absorbed from the soil by root hair cells, by osmosis, and carried up the stem to the leaves in the xylem (the plant's water-carrying tubes). Only a tiny fraction of this water is used in photosynthesis; most evaporates from the leaves in transpiration.
Light comes from the sun, or from artificial lights in greenhouses and laboratories.
Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light. This is why leaves look green: green is the colour the plant isn't using.
Oxygen is partly used by the plant's own cells for respiration. The rest diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata into the air, or into the water for aquatic plants.

The oxygen released comes from splitting water molecules, not from carbon dioxide. This was shown in the 1940s: when plants were given water containing a heavy form (isotope) of oxygen, ¹⁸O, the oxygen gas they released contained ¹⁸O.
Glucose is partly used straight away in the plant's own respiration, which releases its energy as ATP for the cell's work. The rest is turned into sucrose, starch and cellulose.
notes.tip: If asked where the oxygen comes from, say water, not carbon dioxide, and you can back it up with the ¹⁸O evidence. Don't write that plants respire only at night: they respire all the time, day and night.

notes.h: What glucose is turned into: sucrose, starch and cellulose
notes.b: Glucose is a good fuel, but it isn't ideal for moving around the plant, storing or building with. So plants convert it into three other carbohydrates, each suited to one job.
points: Sucrose (for transport): glucose is joined to fructose to form the disaccharide sucrose. Sucrose is carried from the leaves in the phloem (the plant's food-carrying tubes) to growing tips, roots, fruits and storage organs.

Sucrose suits transport because it is soluble, so it travels dissolved in the phloem, and less reactive than glucose. It is not a reducing sugar, so it isn't used up by the cells it passes on the way.

Starch (for storage): glucose is joined into long chains to form the polysaccharide starch. Starch grains build up in the chloroplasts during the day, and longer-term stores are kept in storage organs and seeds, such as potato tubers and cereal grains.
Starch suits storage because it is insoluble, so large amounts can be stored without drawing water into the cell by osmosis, and it is compact.

Cellulose (for building): glucose is joined into the polysaccharide cellulose, which forms the strong walls around plant cells. Because every plant cell has a wall, cellulose is the most abundant organic compound on Earth.
Plants also use glucose to make lipids, such as the oils in seeds, and, combined with nitrates taken from the soil, amino acids for proteins.
notes.tip: Exams ask what happens to the glucose a plant makes. Give its use in respiration, then sucrose for transport in the phloem and starch for storage, each with its reason.

notes.b: When a plant photosynthesises, it pulls carbon out of the air and locks it inside its own body. This is why forests, bogs and the oceans matter in the fight against climate change.
points: A carbon sink is anything that takes in more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases, and stores it. Photosynthesis is the only major biological process that removes carbon dioxide from the air.
The carbon from CO₂ is fixed (built into organic molecules) as glucose, then as sucrose, starch, cellulose and the rest of the plant's body, its biomass.

The carbon stays locked away for as long as the biomass lasts: for decades or centuries in the wood of trees, and for thousands of years in peat bogs, because waterlogged, acidic conditions slow down decomposition.
Algae and phytoplankton (tiny floating photosynthesisers) in the oceans also fix carbon, and some of it is locked up in ocean sediments when they die.
Respiration, decomposition and burning return the stored carbon to the air as CO₂.

Forests, peatlands and the oceans' algae and phytoplankton are the main natural carbon sinks. Cutting down forests, draining or burning peat and burning fossil fuels all release stored carbon and add to the CO₂ that drives climate change.
Fossil fuels are themselves stored photosynthesis: coal, oil and gas hold carbon that plants and algae fixed millions of years ago, which is why burning them adds extra CO₂ to the air.
notes.tip: When explaining the carbon sink role, make the chain clear: CO₂ is taken from the air, fixed into glucose and then into biomass, and stays stored until respiration, decay or burning releases it.

notes.h: Where photosynthesis happens and its two stages
notes.b: Photosynthesis happens inside chloroplasts, and it doesn't happen in one go. It runs as two linked stages in two different parts of the chloroplast: the first captures energy from light, and the second uses that energy to build glucose.
points: In a leaf, most chloroplasts are in the palisade mesophyll cells, just below the upper surface, because that is where light is strongest. Spongy mesophyll cells and guard cells also have some.
Stage 1, the light-dependent stage, takes place on the thylakoid membranes, the flattened sacs inside the chloroplast that are stacked into piles called grana.
1. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
2. The energy is used to split water molecules into oxygen, protons (H⁺) and electrons. This splitting is called photolysis, meaning splitting by light.
3. The oxygen is released as a by-product.
4. The energy is trapped in ATP, and the protons and high-energy electrons are picked up by a hydrogen carrier molecule, ready for stage 2.
Stage 2, the light-independent stage, takes place in the stroma, the fluid that fills the chloroplast around the thylakoids.

1. Carbon dioxide enters the stroma. 2. It is combined with the hydrogen (protons and electrons) brought from stage 1. 3. Energy from the ATP made in stage 1 drives these reactions. 4. Glucose is formed.
notes.tip: Expect to be asked to name the organelle and the exact part of it for each stage: light-dependent on the thylakoids (grana), light-independent in the stroma.

notes.h: How the two stages depend on each other
notes.b: The two stages are like a factory with a delivery service between them. Stage 1 loads up carriers with energy and hydrogen, stage 2 unloads them to build glucose, and the empty carriers go back to be reloaded.
points: Stage 1 supplies the two things stage 2 needs: energy, as ATP, and hydrogen, on the hydrogen carrier.
Stage 2 returns the spent carriers to stage 1: ATP comes back as ADP, and the carrier comes back empty, so both can be reused.
The reactions of stage 2 are controlled by enzymes, which is why this stage, and so the whole process, is affected by temperature.
The light-independent stage doesn't use light directly, but it stops soon after dark, because stage 1 stops and the supply of ATP and hydrogen runs out.
Older books call the light-independent stage the dark stage. That name is misleading: the stage happens in the light, at the same time as stage 1.

Diagram: a chloroplast outline with stage 1 on a thylakoid stack (inputs light and H₂O; output O₂) and stage 2 in the stroma (input CO₂; output glucose → sucrose, starch, cellulose). Arrows: ATP and hydrogen to the stroma; ADP and the empty carrier back.
notes.tip: If asked why the light-independent stage isn't really a "dark" stage, explain that it needs the ATP and hydrogen from the light stage, so it only runs while there is light.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which green plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy, absorbed by chlorophyll, to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
Anything that takes in more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases, storing it; photosynthesis is the only major biological process that removes CO₂ from the air.
The splitting of water molecules using light energy, producing oxygen, protons and electrons.
The first stage of photosynthesis, on the thylakoid membranes, in which light energy splits water and is trapped in ATP and a hydrogen carrier.
The second stage of photosynthesis, in the stroma, in which carbon dioxide is combined with hydrogen and energy from ATP to form glucose.
A disaccharide made of glucose and fructose, which carries carbohydrate from the leaves to other parts of the plant in the phloem.
An insoluble polysaccharide of glucose, used by plants as a compact store of glucose.

questions.prompt: Write a balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis and explain why it is described as an anabolic process.
questions.model: The balanced equation is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, with light energy and chlorophyll written above the arrow. Photosynthesis is anabolic because it builds one large molecule, glucose, from small inorganic molecules, carbon dioxide and water, and it takes in energy, which is supplied by light.

questions.prompt: State the source of each raw material for photosynthesis and what happens to the glucose a plant makes.
questions.model: Carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf through the stomata, mostly on the lower surface, and some comes from the plant's own respiring cells. Water is absorbed from the soil by root hair cells, by osmosis, and carried up to the leaves in the xylem. Light comes from the sun or from artificial light, and is absorbed by chlorophyll. Glucose is used in the plant's own respiration to release energy. The rest is converted: it is joined to fructose to form sucrose, which is transported in the phloem to growing tips, roots, fruits and storage organs; it is joined into starch for storage in the chloroplast and in storage organs such as potato tubers and cereal grains; or it is joined into cellulose, which forms cell walls.

questions.prompt: Outline the two stages of photosynthesis, giving the location of each stage in the chloroplast, and explain how photosynthesis acts as a carbon sink.
questions.model: Stage 1, the light-dependent stage, takes place on the thylakoid membranes of the grana. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which is used to split water molecules into oxygen, protons and electrons. The oxygen is released, the energy is trapped in ATP, and the protons and high-energy electrons are picked up by a carrier molecule. Stage 2, the light-independent stage, takes place in the stroma. Carbon dioxide is combined with the protons and electrons (hydrogen) from stage 1, energy from ATP drives the reactions, which are controlled by enzymes, and glucose is formed. Stage 1 supplies the ATP and hydrogen that stage 2 needs, and stage 2 returns the spent ADP and empty carrier to stage 1. As a carbon sink, photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and fixes it into glucose, and then into sucrose, starch, cellulose and the rest of the plant's biomass. The carbon stays stored while the biomass survives, for example in tree wood for decades or centuries, and in peat bogs for thousands of years, because waterlogged, acidic conditions slow decomposition.
